data.title: Mužla-Čenkov – a Slavic guard hillfort on the bank of the Danube
data.excerpt: In the 9th and 10th centuries a Slavic hillfort stood at the site of Mužla-Čenkov, right on the bank of the Danube; its parts now lie in the localities known as Vilmakert and Orechový sad. It was a multi-period site with a dominant guard and military function, where 271 settlement features, mostly sunken buildings of quadrangular ground plan, were investigated.
data.metaTitle: Mužla-Čenkov – a Slavic hillfort on the Danube
data.metaDescription: A Slavic guard hillfort of the 9th and 10th centuries right on the bank of the Danube; a multi-period site occupied already by the Late Linear Pottery culture.

keyFacts.label: Position
keyFacts.value: The hillfort lies directly on the bank of the Danube, on one of the few markedly raised positions between Štúrovo and Komárno

keyFacts.label: Fortification
keyFacts.value: The Vilmakert locality was enclosed on three sides by a rampart with a surviving length of c. 500 m; on the side towards the Danube it was protected by a steep bank 3 to 5 m high

keyFacts.label: Area
keyFacts.value: The present area of the Vilmakert locality is 2.79 ha; the original extent cannot be determined because of the erosion of the Danube bank

keyFacts.label: Settlement features
keyFacts.value: 271 settlement features were investigated at the hillfort, mostly the remains of sunken buildings of quadrangular ground plan

keyFacts.label: Feature X
keyFacts.value: Inside the hillfort Dr Hanuliak discovered a building of dimensions unique for the Slavic period in the territory of Slovakia, surrounded by graves with rich grave goods

keyFacts.label: Subsistence
keyFacts.value: Archaeozoological results document the keeping of cattle, pigs, in part sheep, goats and poultry, supplemented by hunting and fishing

keyFacts.label: Written sources
keyFacts.value: The Gesta Hungarorum of Simon of Kéza mentions the capture of a stronghold at the ford of Zub, hypothetically linked with Čenkov; a document of 1135 attests „predium in villa Chenka“

timeline.title: The existence of the Slavic hillfort
timeline.description: In the 9th and 10th centuries a Slavic hillfort stood at the site of Mužla-Čenkov, the parts of which now lie in the localities known as Vilmakert and Orechový sad.

timeline.title: The occupation of the site
timeline.description: The site was occupied no later than the second quarter of the 9th century, in a colonising manner, by a larger group of people who were able to build up the chosen area according to a plan and to fortify it with a rampart of solid construction.

timeline.title: The building of the fortification of the first horizon
timeline.description: In connection with the growing tension between the East Frankish and the Great Moravian empires, the system of fortification and the finds of a militant character from the first occupation horizon at the Čenkov hillfort may be linked with this period.

timeline.title: Military clashes and the attachment of territory to Great Moravia
timeline.description: On the basis of the results of military clashes, the territory from Esztergom to Veszprém, the Bakony forest and the lower course of the Rába was attached to the territory of Great Moravia, which may have brought a turn in the functioning of the Čenkov fortified settlement (the second horizon).

timeline.title: The written mention of „villa Chenka“
timeline.description: A now lost document of 1135 mentions „predium in villa Chenka“, which Stephen I granted to one of the ancestors of the Hunt-Poznan family; the designation villa testifies to the loss of the function of the fortification.

timeline.year: second and third thirds of the 10th century
timeline.title: The reduction of occupation in the third horizon
timeline.description: In the third occupation horizon, belonging to the post-Great Moravian period, the concentration of occupation is markedly reduced, with only a small part of the original inhabitants remaining; archaeologists rule out a catastrophic demise through military action.

timeline.title: The fourth period – a small hamlet
timeline.description: The trend of reduced occupation continues into the fourth period as well; features of a small hamlet of dispersed type appear in the original settlement area, recorded in the written sources as villa.

children.text: In the 9th and 10th centuries a Slavic hillfort extended at the site of Mužla-Čenkov, the parts of which now lie in the localities known as Vilmakert and Orechový sad. It can be counted among the hillforts with a dominant guard and military function (Hulínek). The site lies directly on the bank of the Danube. It is a multi-period site, at which occupation of the Late Linear Pottery culture, the Želiezovce group, the Baden culture, the Kosihy-Čaka group, finds from the turn of the Early and Middle Bronze Age, the Vekerzug culture, the La Tène period and the Early Middle Ages – the 9th to 12th centuries – has so far been established. It is one of the few markedly raised positions directly on the bank of the Danube, between Štúrovo and Komárno.

The Vilmakert locality was originally enclosed on three sides by a rampart; on the side towards the Danube there is a steep bank 3 to 5 m high. The present area of the locality is 2.79 ha. The original extent cannot be determined, given the erosion of the bank. The whole area of the site stands out on the ground about 1 m above the surrounding level. As has already been mentioned, the site is enclosed on three sides by a rampart. It is best preserved on the NE side, where it reaches a height of 2 to 3 m above the inner enclosure. On the NW side it was lowered by cultivation and on the W side partly disturbed by the construction of a flood-protection dyke. The shape of the fortification is trapezoidal and the total surviving length is c. 500 m. The original length of the rampart is hard to estimate as a result of the erosion of the Danube bank. On this side, however, in view of the height of the bank, it was not necessary to build the fortification in the same way as towards the interior. It perhaps consisted only of a palisade. The destruction layer of the rampart, made of smaller quarry stones, was uncovered running in a direction outwards from the fortification, as far as the level of the present terrain. In it, however, it was not possible to recognise the front wall unambiguously, as was still the case in the 1950s.

In the section through the fortification the eye is caught by a brown-black layer, running along its whole length and passing smoothly into the ditch. It is relatively compact, but it contains archaeological material from all periods. In all the known profiles the stone destruction layer of the rampart lies on this layer. It is formed of quarry stone of a slate type, easily split. At a distance of 190 cm from its beginning on the inner side of the fortification there were the remains of the front wall, built of larger flat stones laid dry. Its thickness was around 60 cm. Towards the outside of the fortification the height of the destruction layer fell irregularly up to a distance of 400 cm from the front wall. In this part there were larger quarry stones of a sandstone character. It may therefore be supposed that two kinds of material were used in the building of the wall. In the lower part flat, splittable stone, and therefore eminently suitable for this purpose; in the upper part, or rather on the crown of the wall, irregular quarry stone. Practically the whole destruction layer was burnt through, brick-coloured, in places mixed with a considerable quantity of charcoal. Larger pieces of charcoal were found especially around the inner edge of the destruction layer. Only the part in the immediate vicinity of the front wall, up to a height of c. 40 cm, and beneath it was without traces of burning. This would perhaps allow us to consider that the foot of the wall was banked up from the outside. The whole outer part of the destruction layer is covered by a fill of brown soil. Towards the interior of the enclosure, at a distance of 80 cm from the destruction layer, a brown-black bank begins, 500 cm long and 30–60 cm high, separated from the basic layer by a thin little layer of sand. This is evidently an inner berm. It is essentially of the same character as the layer beneath it, but unlike it, it also contains an admixture of fine river gravel. The whole berm is closed off by a fill of lighter brown soil of a sandy character, reaching up to the level of the topsoil. We have relatively insufficient information about the ditch, because for technical reasons it was not possible to investigate it completely. We can only state that it begins at a distance of 610 cm from the front wall.

children.text: Of interest for the question of the origin and the demise of the fortification may be the mention by Simon of Kéza in the well-known book of fables and legends Gesta Hungarorum, concerning the Old Hungarians: “They therefore set out with raised banners, with their women, children and herds, and crossed the Danube at Pest and at the ford of Zub (Szob), and there they captured a certain stronghold in the region of the Danube, in which Svatopluk’s soldiers had gathered, those who had saved themselves by flight when their lord perished.” Even though the trustworthiness of this source is low and is determined by the time of its origin in the years 1282 to 1285 (preserved only in a copy of the 15th century), it must be pointed out that in the case of Čenkov this is so far the only known hillfort in the region of the Danube. On the other hand, no catastrophic horizon was identified at the settlement. Although hypothetically we could link the above report with the site at Čenkov, their unambiguous identification remains more than problematic. A further written report, indirectly connected with the fortification, comes from a now lost document of 1135, where “predium in villa Chenka” is mentioned, which Stephen I granted to one of the ancestors of the Hunt-Poznan family. In the Latin terminology of the 11th–12th centuries the designation villa is used for an unfortified settlement unit with several families, which therefore testifies to the loss of the function of the fortification. The enclosing of the area with a light fence is also assumed.
The internal structure of the built-up area

blocks.caption: Feature X. During the excavation of the Slavic hillfort Dr Hanuliak discovered in its area a building unique in size for the Slavic period in the territory of Slovakia. It stood on a rise inside the hillfort, with several richly furnished graves around it. The building may have had a religious character, but could also have served as a representative building of the nobility. An idol is not documented there. Nor are the posts by the graves, but Dr Hanuliak assumes they may have been there.

children.text: The insights so far into the intensity and quality of the occupation of this site indicate that there was an unusually large concentration of settlement features of the Early Middle Ages (especially the 9th and 10th centuries) here. 271 settlement features were found at the hillfort, mostly the remains of sunken buildings of quadrangular ground plan, of structures and installations, especially heating installations, and of pits, especially grain pits. The arrangement of the buildings most resembles an irregular, clustered type of layout. Detailed analyses of the ground plan of the investigated part of the site led to the conclusion that the building up of the site was probably carried out according to a plan, following previously established rules, among which the main one was the observance of distance relations, that is, of the mutual distances between the individual buildings (between the corners of the buildings), in the process of their founding. The basic unit of occupation was formed by a group of 2–6 houses (families) arranged into planned layout units.
The standing of the inhabitants of the hillfort

The picture of the level of the socio-economic environment of the settlement unit being uncovered takes on a more concrete shape once its connection with the fortification system, consisting of a timber-and-earth rampart with a stone facing and a ditch, has been demonstrated. The settlement formation can then be identified with one of the lowland fortified settlements of the Great Moravian type. The evidence for the higher socio-economic level traditionally associated with this category is not unambiguous. This is partly due to the low number of objects obtained by excavation, such as weapons and parts of warrior equipment, axe-shaped currency bars, bowls of the Silesian type and buckets. Their representatives are usually found in abundance in the contemporary administrative and economic centres and in their settlement agglomerations. The remaining objects of material culture, together with a substantial part of the pottery assemblage of finds, speak rather of the average. Only a less numerous collection of vessels bears the marks of a higher technical and productive perfection of manufacture. The exceptional character of some of its forms and the manner in which the decoration is applied correspond to the higher functional and aesthetic demands of their users and indirectly argue for the environment of a relatively higher stratum. Among this category of finds belongs also the spur that was found, with the parts for fastening the strap. In the grave of this individual, from the category of mounted warriors, traces of the internal fitting out of the grave pit were exceptionally found as well. The other individuals from the graves and from the settlement features belong to the group of averagely to below-averagely equipped. The relative uniformity and the structural simplicity of the buildings, together with the absence of specialised craft installations, likewise testifies to no great economic and social differentiation among the inhabitants of the hillfort.
The subsistence of the inhabitants of the hillfort

Ideas about the productive base of the local community were supplemented by the results of archaeozoological investigations. They brought data on the deliberate keeping of cattle, pigs, in part also of sheep, goats and poultry, supplemented by hunting and fishing. Palaeobotanical analyses, for their part, gave convincing evidence of the predominance of traditional species of cereals. Nor can it be ruled out that these crops were grown in more distant regions and transported to the Čenkov hillfort along trade routes. In a similar way querns and whetstones made of stone raw material exploited in the environment of the middle Hron region were transported to the site. The possibility that agricultural crops were gathered from more distant territory, at the expense of local production, is indirectly indicated by the insights showing that the immediate surroundings of the Čenkov settlement were predominantly wooded. Another point is the sporadic occurrence of agricultural implements, hardly comparable with ideas of intensive agricultural production.
The inhabitants of the hillfort – pagans

Archaeologists state that the recorded manifestations of burial customs, together with the dispersed manner of distributing the graves within the settlement area and with the occurrence of individuals in storage pits, are typical above all of an environment of pagan beliefs. In terms of quality, this is the final stage of paganism, with evidence of the manifestations of crisis that usually appear after the loss of confidence in traditional religious dogmas. Testimony of any kind to the penetrating influence of the new Christian ideology is so far lacking.

On the basis of settlement analyses it can be concluded that the site was occupied no later than the second quarter of the 9th century, in a colonising manner, by a larger group of people. This community of people was little socially stratified, but uniformly organised to such a degree that it was able not only to build up the chosen area according to a plan, but also to fortify it with a rampart of solid construction and massiveness. The development of the occupation of the site itself cannot be interpreted as part or as the culmination of the spontaneous and natural development of the occupation of the local microregion, which until then had been practically unoccupied by the Slavs. The inhumation cemeteries of the period of the Avar Khaganate at Štúrovo, Štúrovo-Obid and Radvaň nad Dunajom came to an end at the close of the 8th century. At Mužla-Čenkov no influence of their material culture was identified. We do not as yet know of any other more pronounced pre-Great Moravian occupation in the immediate vicinity. It was probably a colonising process directed, or rather enabled, by the higher components of the social structure of the time.

The beginnings of the occupation at Čenkov may be connected with the process of the building and the territorial unification of the Principality of Nitra. After reaching such an important frontier divide as the Danube, the founding of a settlement with a military mission for its inhabitants can quite realistically be expected in that area. Besides the demonstration of territorial and state sovereignty by a permanent military garrison, the mission could also have included the monitoring of events in the territory south of the Danube. An increase in the need for this kind of information may be expected especially in the course of the second third of the 9th century. During it, as a result of the development of the political and military ambitions of the East Frankish and the Great Moravian empires, a growth of tension can be observed in their mutual relations. The system of fortification and the finds of a militant character from the first occupation horizon at the Čenkov hillfort may also be linked with the period mentioned.

children.text: The functional centre of gravity of the occupation in the second horizon shifts into the economic sphere (the growing of crops and the keeping of cattle, and also trade in agricultural products), which is documented by the changes in the settlement structure as well. In this period the concentration of dwelling buildings decreased and the number of economic installations, especially grain pits, grew. The turn mentioned in the functioning of the Čenkov fortified settlement may have occurred after the events of 861. On the basis of the results of military clashes, the territory from Esztergom to Veszprém, the Bakony forest and the lower course of the Rába was attached to the territory of Great Moravia. These changes may have been the direct impulse for the disappearance of the original military orientation of the inhabitants of the site under study. Greater importance, by contrast, may have been acquired by the possibility of connecting the opposite banks by means of a river crossing, whose existence in the immediate vicinity of the hillfort has a historical justification. A reflection of further changes in the previous character of the occupation is registered in the third occupation horizon, filling the stretch of the post-Great Moravian period (the second and third thirds of the 10th century). It manifests itself in a marked reduction of the concentration of occupation, when only a small part of the original inhabitants remained here. Archaeologists point out, however, that this was not a catastrophic demise as a result of direct military action from the time of the occupation of present-day Slovakia by members of the Hungarian ethnic group. Any indications for such a consideration are lacking in the find situations. The most recent results of our historiography (Steinhübel) rule out the identification of Čenkov with the hillfort that, according to Simon of Kéza, was captured by the Old Hungarians. The explanation of the marked reduction in the intensity of occupation may hypothetically be presumed to lie in the disappearance of the primary determinants conditioning the original concentration of occupation. The trend of reduced occupation continues into the fourth period as well, belonging broadly to the 11th–12th centuries. In that period features of a small hamlet of dispersed type appear in the original settlement area, recorded in the written sources as villa. In Latin terminology this is a designation for an unfortified unit of agrarian type.
